label: Isometries and Complex Numbers
notes: This chapter, printed pages sixty-five through eighty-two, asks one question: why are Mobius transformations the motion language of hyperbolic geometry? We will treat a point of the hyperbolic plane as a single complex number, and then watch rigid motions become elementary complex arithmetic that preserves the curved metric exactly.

label: The Hyperbolic Plane in Complex Coordinates
notes: A Riemannian metric assigns lengths and angles infinitesimally. The Poincare disk and upper half-plane both record one complex coordinate per point, but rescale the Euclidean ruler by a conformal factor that blows up near the boundary. That single factor encodes all of the negative curvature we are about to exploit.

label: What an Isometry Must Preserve
notes: An isometry is a bijection of the surface that leaves the metric invariant: every infinitesimal length, and therefore every distance, angle, geodesic and area, is reproduced exactly. Our entire strategy is to find all such maps for the hyperbolic plane, and to recognize them as a familiar family of complex functions.

label: Complex Multiplication is a Rotation
notes: Writing a complex number in polar form exposes the geometric content of multiplication. Multiplying by a unit modulus number rotates the plane about the origin by its argument; a general factor also scales by its modulus. This amplitwist is the seed from which every rigid motion of the plane will be assembled.

label: Euclidean Rigid Motions as Complex Maps
notes: Before the curved case, fix intuition in the flat plane. A direct Euclidean isometry is exactly multiplication by a unit complex number followed by a translation: a rotation-translation. Adding a conjugation gives the orientation-reversing reflections. Complex notation has already compressed the whole rigid-motion group into two short formulas.

label: Mobius Transformations
notes: A Mobius transformation sends z to a fractional linear expression with complex coefficients and nonzero determinant. These maps form a group under composition, are determined by their action on three points, and send the family of generalized circles to itself. They are the natural candidates for the isometries we seek.

label: Inversion and Generalized Circles
notes: Every Mobius map factors into translations, a complex scaling, and one inversion in the unit circle. Inversion is the genuinely new ingredient: it swaps inside and outside of the circle and trades lines for circles. Because each factor preserves the family of circles and lines, so does any composition of them.

label: Isometries of the Upper Half-Plane
notes: On the upper half-plane the isometries are precisely the real Mobius transformations, those with real coefficients and positive determinant, together with one reflection. They map the real axis to itself, preserve the imaginary part structure, and therefore leave the hyperbolic metric, with its one over y scaling, completely invariant.

label: Isometries of the Poincare Disk
notes: Transporting the result to the disk, the orientation-preserving isometries become the disk-automorphism Mobius maps: a rotation composed with a so-called Blaschke factor that slides the center to any chosen point. This is the main isometry result, and it makes the homogeneity of hyperbolic geometry visible and computable.

label: Classifying Hyperbolic Motions
notes: Counting fixed points sorts the orientation-preserving isometries into three archetypes. Elliptic maps fix one interior point and rotate around it; parabolic maps fix a single boundary point; hyperbolic maps fix two boundary points and translate along the geodesic joining them. The trace of the matrix decides which type appears.

label: Spacetime and the Lorentz Connection
notes: The same algebra governs special relativity. A Lorentz boost preserves the indefinite spacetime interval just as a hyperbolic isometry preserves hyperbolic distance, and both act as Mobius transformations on a boundary circle or sphere. Complex multiplication thus links the curved metric story to the geometry of light and motion.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: We collapsed rigid motions into complex arithmetic, identified hyperbolic isometries with disk and half-plane Mobius maps, and classified them by fixed points. The recurring lesson is to separate representation from invariant: coordinates and matrices change freely, while preserved distance, the conformal factor, and circle structure carry the real geometry forward.
